list.listitem: Mild hemoptysis is often associated with a respiratory tract infection and can be managed on an outpatient basis with close follow-up. C
The volume and frequency of blood loss is helpful in management decisions but does not indicate the likelihood of malignancy. C

For massive hemoptysis, arteriography with embolization, CTA of chest with IV conract, CT of chest with IV contrast, or chest radiography are appropriate initial tests per ACR guidelines. For non-massive hemoptysis, all of the above with the exception of arteriography are recommended as "usually appropriate". C
Patients with a mass and those at risk for cancer (eg, smokers older than 40 years with hemoptysis for more than 1 week) should have flexible bronchoscopy. B
The overall goals of initial management are bleeding cessation, aspiration prevention, and treatment of the underlying cause. C
Massive hemoptysis requires an expedient and aggressive approach in the ICU in consultation with a pulmonologist and cardiothoracic surgeon as mortality in these patients may be high. C

background.definition: Hemoptysis is expectorating of blood derived from the lungs or bronchial tubes as a result of pulmonary or bronchial hemorrhage. It is divided into massive or nonmassive based on the volume of blood loss; nonmassive hemoptysis is less than 200 mL per day.

list.listitem: A 3-year study of all university hospitals in France (29% of all hospital beds) found 6349 hospitalizations for hemoptysis, of which 2677 did not have a clearly identifiable cause.
There was a strong seasonal trend, with a peak incidence in March and trough in August.
Among 1008 patients with cystic fibrosis who were participating in clinical trials, one or more episodes of hemoptysis occurred in 8%; episodes were more common in adults and 76% were mild.
Among patients with lung cancer, hemoptysis is the presenting symptom in 7% to 10%.
In a Dutch cohort of 74 children with either idiopathic or heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension, hemoptysis occurred in 13 children (17.6%) during a median follow-up of 3.5 years.

Among 1251 patients undergoing percutaneous transthoracic needle biopsy, hemoptysis occurred in 9.5%. Dual antiplatelet therapy increased risk. In two other large case series, hemoptysis occurred in 6.9% of 1153 patients and 1.8% of 1175 cases. In the latter case series, some degree of pulmonary hemorrhage was common (41.1%), but rarely required intervention.
In patients with advanced thyroid cancer treated with antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitors, hemoptysis occurred in 9/140 (6.4%).
Mortality in patients with massive hemoptysis in the setting of lung cancer is 59% to 100%, higher than of hemoptysis from other causes.
See Differential Diagnosis table. The cause is undetermined (idiopathic hemoptysis) in up to 34% of cases.

In general, the list of conditions that can produce hemoptysis is broad and can include infection, malignancy, inflammatory and autoimmune disease, cardiovascular disease, trauma, foreign body aspiration, transthoracic procedures, coagulopathy, and rare causes such as pulmonary endometriosis and idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis.

A UK outpatient series found that the most common reasons for hemoptysis were acute respiratory tract infection (64%), asthma (10%), COPD (8%), lung cancer (6%), bronchiectasis (2%), pulmonary embolism (1%), tuberculosis (0.4%) and bleeding disorder (0.3%).

In a systematic review of 7 studies of hemoptysis in children, specific etiologies (found in 89%) included infection such as pneumonia, bronchitis, and pulmonary tuberculosis (37.6%), heart disease (6.4%), and neoplasia (4%).
See for the frequency of different causes in different geographic settings.
The lungs receive blood from the pulmonary and bronchial arterial systems.
The low pressure pulmonary system typically produces small volume hemoptysis.
The bronchial system, at systemic pressure, produces profuse bleeding.
Infection causes superficial mucosal inflammation leading to rupture of superficial blood vessels.
Cancer may cause superficial mucosal invasion, erosion into blood vessels, or highly vascular lesions.
The volume and frequency of blood loss is helpful in management decisions but does not help in the diagnosis or incidence of cancer. C

For massive hemoptysis, arteriography with embolization, CTA of chest with IV contrast, or CT of chest with IV contrast are appropriate initial tests per ACR guidelines. For non-massive hemoptysis, all of the above with the exception of arteriography are recommended as "usually appropriate". C
CT is more sensitive than bronchoscopy for the detection of lung cancer in patients with non-massive hemoptysis., C
Patients with a mass and those at risk for cancer (men older than 40 years, smoking history greater than 40 pack-years, and duration of hemoptysis >1 week) should have flexible bronchoscopy. C
Smokers older than 40 years who have unexplained hemoptysis should be monitored losely. C

list.listitem: It is important to distinguish hemoptysis from hematemesis. Patients with the latter typically have nausea and vomiting, as well as a history of gastric or liver disease. The sputum is more likely to have a coffee ground appearance with a brown/black color. In hemoptysis the coughed up material is typically bright red or pink in color, and may be frothy, liquid, or clotted. There is more often a history of heart or lung disease, and patients may have a feeling of asphyxiation.
History and physical examination clues to the causes of hemoptysis are shown in the differential diagnosis table.

Ask about signs and symptoms of infection (eg, fever, cough, sputum production, facial pain), malignancy (eg, cachexia, weight loss, tobacco history), trauma or foreign body ingestion, and immune deficiency. Always consider pulmonary embolism (PE), and inquire about risk factors such as recent surgery, travel, or immobilization.
Determine current medication use, in particular anticoagulants, NSAIDs, and antithrombotics.
Renal failure or hematuria suggests Goodpasture's syndrome, while patients with Wegener's granulomatosis may have associated nasal or oral symptoms.
Symptoms associated with menses suggest pulmonary endometriosis.
A careful travel and social history may reveal risk factors for tuberculosis, parasitic diseases, and zoonoses.
Chronic cough, dyspnea, and/or sputum production suggests chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or bronchiectasis.
With respect lung cancer as a cause, the positive predictive value for hemoptysis increases from 8.4% in patients aged 55 years to 20.4% in those 85 years and older.
Obtain CBC to establish degree of blood loss and evaluate for thrombocytopenia.

The material coughed up with hemoptysis is typically alkaline, and may have a frothy, liquid, or clotted appearance. On microscopic examination, macrophages and neutrophils may be seen. In hematemesis, the pH of vomitus is acidic and may be mixed with food particles.
Imaging is required for all new episodes of hemoptysis, ideally within 2 weeks.
For massive hemoptysis, ACR guidelines recommend arteriography with embolization, CTA of chest with IV conract, CT of chest with IV contrast, or chest radiography as "usually appropriate".
For non-massive hemoptysis, all of the above with the exception of arteriography are recommended as "usually appropriate".
For recurrent hemoptysis, ACR guidance recommends CXR, arteriography with embolizaiton, or CTA of chest with IV contrast as usually appropriate.
See differential diagnosis table for typical findings of different conditions, such as mass, infiltrate, cavitary lesions, and nodules.
If CXR is the initial imaging, patients with evidence of parenchymal disease on CXR or with risk factors for cancer such as tobacco use or occupational exposures should have high resolution chest CT.
If this evaluation is negative but symptoms persist, CT angiography or bronchoscopy should be considered. Patients with a mass on CXR or CT should also have flexible bronchoscopy.

In patients with non-massive hemoptysis, a systematic review of 11 studies with 2015 patients concluded that CT scan was more sensitive than fiberoptic bronchoscopy for detection of lung cancer (98% vs 86%). A second systematic review confirmed this, finding higher sensitivity for CT scan than for bronchoscopy (99% vs 84%) and equally high specificity for both tests (99% to 100%).
Patients should also undergo blood typing and cross-match, coagulation studies, renal function testing, and sputum testing for acid-fast bacilli, fungal cultures, and cytology.
The use of high-resolution CT with bronchoscopy gives a greater positive yield of pathology for the diagnosis of hemoptysis than either study alone.

Patients with recurrent or unexplained hemoptysis may need additional laboratory tests. This includes purified protein derivative test (PPD), and sputum for acid-fast bacilli, gram stain, and culture (infection); sputum cytology and bronchoscopy (malignancy); prothrombin time/partial thromboplastin time/international normalized ratio (INR) (coagulopathy), d-dimer (VTE); b-natriuretic peptide or echocardiogram (heart failure, mitral stenosis); arterial blood gas (hypoxia); and sedimentation rate (autoimmune disease or malignancy).

In a single study of 81 patients with cryptogenic hemoptysis (no obvious cause after initial evaluation with CXR, bronchoscopy and chest CT), no cancer was identified after a 48-month follow-up period. Such patients may have Dieulafoy disease (a large tortuous arteriole in the stomach; uncommon).
For the evaluation of nonmassive hemoptysis see .

Consider ICU admission or referral to a specialty center for patients with: (1) respiratory impairment (RR > 30 breaths/minute, oxygen saturation < 88% on RA), (2) hemodynamic instability (hemoglobin < 8 g/dl or rapid blood loss), (3) massive hemoptysis defined as more than 200 ml/48 hours or more than 50 ml per episode in patients with COPD, (4) patients with COPD, cystic fibrosis, or history of pneumonectomy), and (5) other serious comorbidities such as ongoing need for anticoagulation or coronary artery disease.

Massive hemoptysis requires an expedient and aggressive approach in the ICU in consultation with a pulmonologist and cardiothoracic surgeon. Securing the airway and maintaining adequate oxygenation is paramount, usually requiring endotracheal intubation and endobronchial management. Selective right or left mainstem intubation may be necessary to protect the non-bleeding lung.
The mortality in massive hemoptysis depends on the bleeding rate and etiology: patients with malignancy and hemoptysis of >1000 mL in 24 hours have a mortality of up to 80%.
Airway maintenance is critical in massive hemoptysis since the cause of death is asphyxiation not exsanguination.
Treatment for specific conditions can be found in the chapters on those conditions.
Antifibrinolytics may reduce duration of bleeding in patients with hemoptysis, but data are limited.

Recommendations for the management of hemoptysis in patients with cystic fibrosis regarding hospitalization and use of antibiotics and embolization can be found in the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation Pulmonary Therapies Committee guideline.

For patients with massive hemoptysis from lung cancer, once the airway is secure, bronchoscopy is used to identify and treat the bleeding site, if identified, using laser or argon plasma photocoagulation or electrocautery. Methods to arrest the bleeding with an unidentified source include tamponade with bronchoscopic wedging, balloon, or mesh; instillation of iced saline or vasoactive substances; or bronchial artery embolization. For patients with unresectable lung cancer with non-massive hemoptysis, external beam radiotherapy can be used or endobronchial brachytherapy for intraluminal tumors.

An Indian study randomized 110 patients with hemoptysis to IV or nebulized tranexamic acid, and found somewhat better hemostasis at 30 minutes with the nebulized version (73% vs 51%, p = 0.002, NNT = 5). A systematic review identified 3 RCTs with 351 patients comparing inhaled tranexamic acid with placebo for non-massive hemoptysis. The relative risk for hemostasis was 3.85.

A systematic review identified 3 RCTs and 9 cohort studies with 1231 patients comparing bronchial artery embolization (BAE) with usual care. Patients receiving BAE had lower rates of recurrence (26.5% vs 34.6%, NNT = 11), higher clinical success rates (92% vs 81%, NNT = 9) and lower mortality due to hemoptysis (.8% vs 3.2%, NNT = 42). All cause mortality was not affected. Rates of major complications were 0.2% and minor complications were 15.6%.

Recurrence of hemoptysis after arterial embolization is common. In one case series, noted above, recurrent hemoptysis occurred in 40% and one third died during follow-up. One third died during follow-up. In another case series, also noted above, recurrence at 1 year occurred in about a quarter of patients with benign disease (28/108) and in most patients with cancer (30/46).

Surgery conducted for massive hemoptysis from pulmonary tuberculosis in 89 patients was successful in all but 2 who died; intraoperative morbidity rate was 31.5% and only two had recurrent hemoptysis.

Using the Nationwide Inpatient Sample database of 457,523 admissions for hemoptysis, 2,671 patients (0.58%) underwent major lung resection. Mortality was 15.2% after pneumonectomy and 6.6% after lobectomy.
